findings.title: Convergence assertion (5.2) can pass whether or not herding works
findings.description:
The slice says "the herd's mean heading converges toward the leaders' initial heading" (slice line 389-391). Task 5.2 only asserts that the mean heading at the end "has positive x-component."

At tick 0, five of the 50 agents already move at `[4.0, 0.0]`, while the other 45 have random velocities that average out to roughly zero. So the population mean already has a positive x-component before any forces run. The assertion is nearly guaranteed to pass, even with `leadership_weight=0`. The step also leaves "mean heading" undefined: it could mean the average of unit heading vectors or the direction of the mean velocity.

Fix:
- Define the metric exactly. For example: the average of each agent's unit heading vector, taken only over the 45 non-leaders.
- Assert it against a threshold or against the value at tick 0. For example: non-leader mean heading x-component at tick 300 > the same quantity at tick 0 + margin, or the angle to `[1, 0]` is below a stated bound.

findings.title: Differentiation test (5.3) lets the implementer pick whichever metric passes
findings.description:
5.3 asserts "herding heading variance < flocking heading variance, **or** herding mean eastward component > flocking mean eastward component." An implementer can choose whichever comparison happens to pass for seed 42. That makes the test unfalsifiable in practice. It also leaves a junior implementer with an open design decision.

The slice's verification walkthrough (slice line 474-476) expects **both**: lower heading variance **and** an eastward bias. Name one metric to assert, or require both, and define how heading variance is computed (circular variance of the heading angles is the usual choice). "Statistically measurable" with a single seed is not really statistical. Either drop that wording or say the assertion is a fixed-seed regression check.

findings.title: "No nested Python loops" requirement not carried into the tasks
findings.description:
The slice lists as a technical requirement: "Both forces are vectorized within each agent's neighborhood — no nested Python loops" (slice line 395-396). Task 4.1 writes the weighted heading as `sum(velocity[i] * leadership[i]) / sum(leadership)`. That index-style pseudocode invites an inner Python loop over neighbors, and no step states or checks the constraint.

Add to 4.1 an explicit step: compute the weighted average with NumPy over `state.velocities[neighbors]` and `state.leadership[neighbors]`, e.g. `(lead[:, None] * vel).sum(axis=0) / lead.sum()`, with no loop over neighbors. Also add a line to 3.1. MomentumForce can drop the per-agent loop entirely and compute `velocities[idx] * momentum_weight` directly. Note that `heading * speed` is just `velocity`, so the force reduces to that.

findings.title: Commit points are checkbox tasks instead of plain `**Commit**:` markers
findings.description:
Tasks 1.3, 2.3, 3.3, 4.3, 5.4 and 6.3 are checkbox items (e.g. `- [ ] **1.3 Commit: extend AgentState**`). Commit markers should be plain `**Commit**:` lines, never checkboxes. Where they sit is right: each follows a tested, working unit. Only the format is wrong.

Task 6.3 (lines 180-182) is a different problem. After 5.4, the only remaining changes are check-offs, so 6.3 would be a commit that only checks boxes. Remove it, and let check-offs ride along with the 5.4 commit.

findings.title: Hand-constructed LeadershipForce test lacks an exact expected value
findings.description:
The success criterion "each force produces the correct output for hand-constructed inputs" is met exactly for MomentumForce (line 96: `≈ [3.0, 0.0]`). For LeadershipForce, the test only checks "biases toward agent 1's heading."

The expected value is easy to compute. Agent 2 is stationary, so the weighted heading is `(0.1·[0,1] + 0.9·[1,0]) / 1.0 = [0.9, 0.1]`, and with `leadership_weight=1.0` the force is `[0.9, 0.1]`. Assert that value with `np.allclose`.

Likewise, the uniform-leadership test (line 127) says "similar to plain velocity averaging." The two should be identical when leadership is uniform, so assert equality with the mean neighbor velocity minus the agent's own velocity.

findings.title: Redundant protocol and integration checks
findings.description:
- **Protocol conformance is checked three times.** It appears in the implementation verify steps (3.1 line 91, 4.1 line 122), again as unit tests (3.2 line 95, 4.2 line 125), and again in 6.2. Delete 6.2 and the inline verify lines; the unit tests are enough.
- **5.1 duplicates 5.2.** The "runs without error" test in 5.1 (lines 141-145) is fully covered by 5.2, which runs `tick()` with all five forces for 300 ticks. 5.1's "confirm forces interact correctly" has no assertion. Merge 5.1 into 5.2, or cut it.
- **6.1's warnings check is vague.** "No warnings about missing fields or deprecated patterns" (line 174) cannot be verified as written. Drop it, or make it concrete (e.g. `-W error`).

findings.title: Epsilon given as an inline example value
findings.description: Tasks 3.1 and 4.1 (line 117) each write "epsilon (e.g. 1e-10)." The project rules say to avoid hard-coded constants and duplicated values. Specify one module-level constant in `herding.py`, shared by both forces, so the implementer doesn't put the literal inline in two places.
